chapter: Records, dances and Blanche Calloway (repeated passages)
title: Trumbauer's rhythm, his Tiger Rag solo and playing on changes
summary: They discuss Trumbauer's rhythm, his Tiger Rag solo that saxophonists admired, and that playing on changes was around early.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: The fact that Trumbauer didn't really swing much... I mean, he...when he played something in the tempo of, like, "Singing The Blues," it didn't matter too much. But other tempos, there seems to be kind of a funny kind of rhythm there that sounds a little corny at times. But that didn't matter too much, apparently, in the way he was appreciated anyhow.

I remember a piece(?) (now, I don't know what the name of it was, but it was based on "Tiger Rag") that Frankie Trumbauer played, and it was a real great solo. And all the saxophone players dug it. It went like this: [SINGS SOLO VERBATIM] Do you remember that one?

That's "Tromb..." I don't know whether it is or not. But he didn't sound... He sounded as modern in them times... In fact, that sounds good now, you know, if you play it. So what are you going to do with that? Right?
That's playing with a lot of changes. So that was already pretty much a way of playing then. Sometimes people seem to think that playing on changes didn't come in until later on...
Sure. Bix Beiderbecke's 'I'm Comin', Virginia' was real great. You know?
